Apple accused a new UK proposal targeting App Store fees as de facto price control today, warning it could harm innovation and investment. Here's what we know.

Apple fights back against UK App Store regulation

According to Reuters, Apple officially filed its response today to a consultation from the UK's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), opposing a proposed rule that would allow app developers to link to alternative payment options.

The CMA was able to impose this requirement after designating Apple and Google as having "strategic market status" in their respective mobile platform markets last year. Under the UK's new digital markets regime, this designation allows regulators to introduce company-specific rules to promote competition and give consumers more choice.

Under the proposal, Apple and Google could still collect commissions from developers who complete transactions through alternative payment methods, but any associated fees must be considered "fair and reasonable."

Reuters noted that the CMA "expects the steering fees to be lower than current App Store charges, with the savings passed on to UK consumers or reinvested in developers' businesses to support innovation."

Apple, however, disagrees and is actively opposing the proposal. According to Reuters:

and

The CMA refused to accept Apple's characterization of the proposal as price control, saying its intention was to set principles for judging whether steering fees are fair and reasonable, rather than directly setting the level of such fees.
